planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring into consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in deep shade; like the species, this selection resents drying out and declines in neutral or alkaline ground.

directions: An RHS-recognized selection of deer fern, also listed under the older synonym 'Incisa', distinguished from the typical species by pinnae with jagged, saw-toothed margins rather than the smooth-edged fronds of wild plants. It shares the species' dimorphic habit of flat, spreading sterile fronds beneath upright, narrower fertile fronds, and the same strict requirement for cool, consistently moist, acidic soil in full shade. It is best suited to Pacific Northwest, Pacific Coast, or cool coastal Atlantic gardens, where it adds a finer-textured, ragged-edged variant to shaded fern plantings.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in full shade; crested forms of deer fern are slower to bulk up than the plain species and benefit from undisturbed, consistently damp crowns.

directions: An RHS-recognized crested selection of deer fern, in which the frond tips branch and fork into small tasseled crests instead of tapering to a plain point, giving an otherwise strictly linear fern a softer, more ornamental silhouette. It retains the species' distinctive two-part habit — flat sterile fronds surrounding upright fertile ones — and the same demand for acidic, humus-rich soil that stays reliably moist. Best grown in cool, shaded woodland conditions along the Pacific Coast or in mild, humid coastal gardens where summer heat and drought are not extreme.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in spring into humus-rich, gritty, alkaline to neutral soil in full to partial shade; some filtered light brings out the best golden spring color without scorching the fronds.

directions: A Crispum Group selection of hart's tongue fern distinguished by deeply ruffled, wavy-margined fronds that emerge a rich yellow in spring before darkening to green by late summer, with the gold color most pronounced in some filtered light since direct sun scorches the leaves and deep shade leaves them plain green. Like the species, it needs alkaline to neutral, gritty, humus-rich soil kept evenly moist but well-drained, and declines quickly in acidic ground. Crispum Group plants are usually sterile and are propagated only by division, so its ruffled, seasonally gold-tinted form stays a comparatively uncommon sight among the many hart's tongue cultivars grown in shaded limestone or formal woodland borders.
